Estimates are that 40% of the world have not experienced darkness at levels below moonlight (Swaddle et al., 2015). All animals with a visual system are impacted by the presence of light at night. Typically, these issues are related to attraction and disorientation (Allen, 1880). There are other issues, however, that impact breeding, feeding, and behavior. As an example, the timing of morning song in robins is significantly impacted by the proximity to a roadway lighting installation (Kempnenaers et al., 2010), as shown in Figure 11. Figure 11: Impact of lighting on timing of birdsong (dark blue in unlighted areas and light blue in lighted areas) (Kempnenaers et al., 2010). Here, the light blue points represent birds that are close to an area with artificial light at night, and the dark blue points are those not exposed to light. The metric is the number of minutes of the start of song relative to sunrise. While the song is obviously earlier, another impact of the proximity to roadway lighting is that the birds located closer to lighting also increased their probability of siring offspring. 25 These impacts are not just limited to birds. The impact on sea turtles has been long known (Sella et al., 2006). Similarly, mammals, fish and insects are all impacted by artificial light at night (Brüning et al., 2016). There is extensive literature on this topic; a complete literature review would be significant, but a primer on this topic is provided in Rich and Longcore (Rich & Longcore, 2006) A method to assess the impact of the lighting is provided by Longcore (Longcore et al., 2018a). Here the actinic (activating) spectrum for a variety of effects is considered. These are shown in Figure 12 for a variety of animals and effects, including the human response, the melanopic response, and sky glow impacts. Figure 12: Actinic curves for a variety of effects from (Longcore et al., 2018a). These curves are then convolved with the spectrum of the light source to provide an estimate of the effect. Longcore performed this calculation for a variety of light sources, and the results are shown in Figure 13 as a ratio to the daylight impact. It should be noted that some of these light sources are experimental; however, the process of evaluating the spectra would remain the same. 26 Figure 13. Sample impacts of a variety of light sources on selected responses (Longcore et al., 2018a). In most cases, lower CCT had a lower impact on the metric of interest. A calculation worksheet is available online (Longcore et al., 2018b). 2.2.3.3.2 Plants and Vegetation Similar to the effects on wildlife, roadway lighting generally tends to have an effect on the plants that need a dark cycle to reach maturity, like soybeans.
